title: Understanding Self-Supervised Learning via Latent Distribution Matching
claim: Representation learning can be cast as matching a transformed data distribution to a latent model, splitting the loss into alignment and uniformity.
layout: Left images feed dashed arrows to a right sphere; loss equation box below
description: On the left, a brace groups two similar photos of a coot, labeled P_data(x,x'). Below them is a stack of blue-bordered images of a different animal, a hyrax, labeled P_data(x⁻) as negative samples. Dashed black arrows labeled R(z|x) and R(z'|x') carry the paired images to a gray 3D sphere standing for the latent space. Blue dots are spread across the sphere. Two black points sit close together inside a red glow, joined by a short red arrow for alignment. Blue arrows push the nearby points apart for uniformity. A dashed blue arrow carries the negatives onto the sphere. A formula above the sphere defines R(z,z'). A boxed equation at the bottom writes F as a negative KL divergence. It splits into a red alignment term, a gray marginal term and a blue entropy term. The eye goes first to the sphere with its red glow.
caption: We formulate SSL as a distribution matching problem in which the transformed data distribution $R(z,z')$ is matched to the latent model $P_\theta(z,z')$. The transformation is deterministic $R(z|x)=\delta(z-f(x))$, where $f(x)$ is a deep network. The model likelihood $\log P_\theta$ and latent entropy $H_R$ correspond to alignment and uniformity terms in the loss function [ref].
abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) excels at finding general-purpose latent representations from complex data, yet lacks a unifying theoretical framework that explains the diverse existing methods and guides the design of new ones. We cast SSL as latent distribution matching (LDM): learning representations that maximize their log-probability under an assumed latent model (alignment), while maximizing latent entropy to prevent collapse (uniformity). This view unifies independent component analysis with contrastive, non-contrastive, and predictive SSL methods, including stop gradient approaches. Leveraging LDM, we derive a nonlinear, sampling-free Bayesian filtering model with a Kalman-based predictor for high-dimensional timeseries. We further prove that predictive LDM yields identifiable latent representations under mild assumptions, even with nonlinear predictors. Overall, LDM clarifies the assumptions behind established SSL methods and provides principled guidance for developing new approaches.
